title: Int32Array.prototype.sort() sorts numerically by default; Array.prototype.sort() on the same numbers doesn't
assumption: sort() means the same thing on every array-like object in JavaScript — if plain arrays sort numbers as strings by default, typed arrays must too.

input.description: Converting a plain array of numbers to a typed array (common when passing data to WebGL, audio buffers, or any binary-protocol code) and calling the same-named .sort() method on it with no comparator.

what_goes_wrong: The plain array's default sort() returns [1, 10, 2, 9] (string order, the usual trap). The typed array's default sort() on the identical numbers returns [1, 2, 9, 10] — correctly ascending numeric order — with no comparator passed at all. The exact same method name, called the same way, defaults to opposite comparison strategies depending only on which kind of array it's called on.
why: The ECMAScript spec gives %TypedArray%.prototype.sort its own default comparison, defined numerically: smaller values first, -0 before +0, and NaN (possible in Float32Array/Float64Array) at the end. Typed arrays can only hold numbers (or BigInts), so there is no need for the string fallback. Array.prototype.sort's default has to work for arrays holding any mix of values, and the spec defines it with ToString instead. Python's sorted() on a list of ints always compares the integer values, so there is no equivalent split.
fix: Don't assume .sort()'s default behavior transfers between plain arrays and typed arrays, or rely on that difference — pass an explicit numeric comparator to Array.prototype.sort() regardless, so the code reads the same way (and behaves the same way) whichever kind of array it ends up operating on.
